questions.prompt: Put the lockout/tagout steps in order: match each step number to its step.

pairs.right: Prepare and notify the people affected
Shut the machine down with its normal controls
Isolate it from every energy source
Apply your own lock and tag

questions.explanation: Prepare and notify, shut down, isolate, lock and tag, release stored energy, then verify zero energy before you start work.

questions.prompt: Why is an emergency stop **not** a lockout?
options: It is a control: a reset, a fault or another person can start the machine again
It takes too long to press
It only works on DC machines
It turns off the lights as well
questions.explanation: An e-stop stops the machine but does not isolate it from its energy. Only a lock on the isolating device, with your key, keeps it from starting.

questions.prompt: When you check for voltage with a meter, why do you test the meter on a known live source **again after** testing the circuit?
options: To prove the meter did not fail during the check, so its "dead" reading can be trusted
Because the first test is only for AC
questions.explanation: Live-dead-live: if the meter fails, it reads "dead" on a live circuit. Testing it on a live source before and after proves it was working.

questions.prompt: Which of these can injure you at an electrical panel? Choose every one that is.
options: Shock from touching a live part
Arc flash, even without touching anything
Nothing, once the PLC program is stopped
questions.explanation: Shock, arc flash and burns are the main electrical hazards. Stopping the PLC program does not remove power from the panel.

questions.prompt: Which OSHA regulation requires lockout/tagout when servicing machines?
options: 29 CFR 1910.147, the control of hazardous energy
questions.explanation: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147 is the lockout/tagout regulation. NFPA 70E is the electrical safety standard (a standard, not an OSHA regulation), and IEC 61131-3 is the PLC programming standard.
